read: full: pp. 1-6 (abstract to conclusions) and appendices A.1-A.3 (pp. 9-12) read; reference list and prompt tables (pp. 6-8, 12-17) skimmed
venue_now: arXiv only: the text file is arXiv 2404.18796v2, 1 May 2024 (page 1 footer); notes/search_llm_judge.md found no peer-reviewed venue as of 2026-10-01
what_it_is: A Cohere study proposing to replace a single large LLM judge (typically GPT-4) with a Panel of LLm evaluators (PoLL): several smaller judges from disjoint model families, whose independent scores are pooled by a voting function (pp. 1-2). The panel used is Command R, Claude 3 Haiku and GPT-3.5, with max voting on binary QA correctness judgements and average pooling on 1-5 Chatbot Arena scores (p. 3). Across three settings and six datasets (KILT Natural Questions, TriviaQA and HotpotQA single-hop; Bamboogle and HotpotQA multi-hop; Chatbot Arena Hard), the panel agrees with human judgements better than GPT-4 alone, shows less intra-model bias, and costs seven to eight times less (pp. 1, 4-6). In the QA settings the judged task is reference-based: whether the short gold answer is semantically contained in a model's answer (pp. 4-5).
domain: LLM-as-a-judge evaluation of open-domain and multi-hop QA answers and of chatbot responses
size: 6 datasets in 3 settings (p. 2); human-annotated examples: NQ 688, TriviaQA 316, HotpotQA single-hop 784, HotpotQA multi-hop 595, Bamboogle 750 (p. 12, Table 8); Arena Hard, 500 prompts (p. 3); 6 to 9 evaluated models per setting; 3 panel judges, with GPT-4 as the single-judge comparison
source_of_items: existing datasets (KILT versions of NQ, TriviaQA and HotpotQA; Bamboogle; the 500 mined Chatbot Arena prompts of Arena Hard), answered by the evaluated models, with new human correctness labels for the QA settings (pp. 3-4, 9-12)
has_gold_traces: no: short human reference answers for QA (p. 3); the crowd-sourced Chatbot Arena rankings serve as ground truth for Arena Hard (pp. 3-4)
evaluation: LLM judge, which is the object of study: reference-based binary correctness for QA and pairwise preference for Arena Hard (pp. 2-4). The judges are scored by Cohen's kappa against human labels (p. 4), by Pearson and Kendall tau against the Chatbot Arena ranking (p. 4), and by their accuracy deviations from human labels (p. 5).
human_validation: Cohere's internal professional annotators (novelists, copywriters, copy editors, journalists) judged whether the reference answer was semantically contained in each generated answer; NQ and single-hop HotpotQA were triple-annotated and pooled by majority vote, the other sets single-annotated (pp. 4, 11-12). No agreement among the human annotators is reported. Arena Hard uses crowd-sourced Chatbot Arena rankings as ground truth (pp. 3-4).

engtrace_use.sentence: Stage 1: Automated AI Pre-Screening. Building upon the 'Panel of LLM' (PoLL) methodology (Verga et al., 2024), we construct an 'AI Tribunal' comprising three frontier reasoning models: GPT-5 (OpenAI, 2025a), Claude Opus 4.5 (Anthropic, 2025b), and Gemini 3 (Google, 2025). (section 3.3, L260-265)
engtrace_use.explanation: The sentence attributes to Verga et al. a method of pooling several independent LLM judges, and the paper proposes exactly that: each judge scores independently and a voting function pools the scores (p. 2), with judges drawn from disjoint families to reduce intra-model bias (pp. 1-3). The Tribunal (three judges from three developers, pooled by median and majority vote) is a fair adaptation, and the sentence claims nothing about PoLL beyond its name. Three caveats belong in the revision rather than in the verdict: (1) the paper's expansion is 'Panel of LLm evaluators' (pp. 1-2), not 'Panel of LLM'; (2) the Tribunal drops PoLL's other defining choice, a larger number of smaller and cheaper judges in place of one large model (pp. 1, 6), by using three frontier models; (3) PoLL's evidence covers reference-based QA correctness and chatbot preference rankings, and its authors say its applicability to 'math or reasoning evaluations' is untested (p. 6). So 'building upon' must not be read as PoLL having validated a panel for auditing engineering templates or for judging reasoning steps; the May paper also used the Tribunal as its Tier 2 step judge (L505-508).

suggested_wording: Following PoLL (Verga et al., 2024), whose panel of three smaller judges from different model families agreed with human correctness labels better than a single GPT-4 judge on three QA datasets and showed less intra-model bias, the template screen pools three judges from different developers, none of them on the evaluated roster.
facts_to_cite: PoLL scores an output with several judges from different model families, each scoring independently, and pools their scores with a voting function (p. 2); the panel used is Command R, Claude 3 Haiku and GPT-3.5 (p. 3).

Against human correctness labels on KILT single-hop QA, the panel's Cohen's kappa was 0.763 (NQ), 0.906 (TriviaQA) and 0.867 (HotpotQA), against GPT-4's 0.627, 0.841 and 0.830; Haiku alone scored 0.873 on HotpotQA (p. 4, Table 1).
On Chatbot Arena Hard, the panel's model ranking correlated with the Chatbot Arena leaderboard at Pearson 0.917 and Kendall tau 0.778, against GPT-4's 0.817 and 0.667 (p. 4, Table 2).
A single judge's agreement depends on its prompt: GPT-4's kappa on NQ ranged from 0.518 (zero-shot) to 0.725 (with an instruction not to 'overthink') (p. 5, Table 3).

Intra-model bias: on the multi-hop sets, each evaluated model received its largest positive deviation from the human labels when judged by itself (p. 5), and the GPT-4 judge ranked another GPT-4 variant second on Arena Hard, against fourth in Chatbot Arena (p. 5).
The panel's accuracy deviations from human labels had the smallest spread (standard deviation 2.2, against 6.1 for GPT-3.5) (p. 5).
The three-model panel was seven to eight times cheaper to run than a single GPT-4 Turbo judge (p. 6).
The authors call for further work on whether the method applies to math or reasoning evaluations, and leave panel selection to future work (p. 6).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: judging with models from several families to limit family bias, which EngTrace applies in its Layer 1 template screen (three judges from outside the roster) and in its roster rule (no judge model is evaluated); reference-based judging against a gold answer, as EngTrace's residual judge checks a trace against gold milestones; and validation of judges against human labels with chance-corrected agreement. Lacks: reasoning traces or step-level judging (the judges see final answers, p. 4); quantitative or engineering content (open-domain QA and chat); generated instances; expert annotators (professional writers and editors, p. 11); agreement figures among the human annotators; and any test on math or reasoning, which the authors flag as open (p. 6).
notes: Batch V question: of the five papers in this batch, PoLL bears most on the planned judge-validity paragraph. It offers three usable findings: a single judge favours its own model's outputs (p. 5; the paper also cites Panickssery et al. 2024 for self-preference, p. 2); a single judge's agreement with humans moves with prompt wording (kappa 0.518 to 0.725 for GPT-4, p. 5); and a panel of diverse smaller judges agreed with human labels better than GPT-4 alone, at seven to eight times lower cost (pp. 4, 6). Its limits matter as much: all its evidence is on reference-based QA correctness, which the authors call 'essentially a fuzzy string matching exercise' (p. 5), and on chatbot preference, and they flag math and reasoning as untested (p. 6). Since the AI Tribunal is now only the Layer 1 template screen (Grok 4.6, MiniMax M3, MiMo-V2.5-Pro, all from outside the roster), the revised text may cite PoLL for that screen's panel design, and for the self-preference and prompt-sensitivity evidence that motivates the roster rule (D-110). It should not cite PoLL as validating the screen: the screen's validity is EngTrace's own Layer 2 evidence (a 10.2% false-positive rate against the experts; 34 of 45 Pass 1 claims confirmed; state brief section 1). A tension to address: the residual judge is a single model (MiMo), the very setup PoLL argues against. The revised text should say why one judge suffices: MiMo sees only the residue the deterministic checks leave (0.112 to 0.252 of milestones per model), it comes from a family not on the roster, and it was validated against experts (E5 milestone F1 0.958 on X1). It should not claim that a panel would remove bias: the LLM-judge search note records later work that contests PoLL's independence assumption (correlated errors across judges; ensembling reduces self-preference but does not remove it). Name: the May text expands PoLL as 'Panel of LLM'; the paper's expansion is 'Panel of LLm evaluators' (pp. 1-2). Reference entry: the authors match the arXiv record, though the printed 'Hofstatter' drops the umlaut of the paper's spelling (p. 1); cite it as an arXiv preprint.
